# How to use this guide

Pharmacognosy and Phytochemistry I is a descriptive subject: marks come from clear definitions, neat classifications, correct biological sources and well-labelled tables and diagrams. Study one unit a day. Read the notes, then close them and write out every classification table and every drug monograph (source, family, chemistry, tests, uses) from memory. Finish with the question bank and the MCQs for that unit.

The five units follow the five units of the PCI syllabus exactly. Unit 5 is the longest because it covers many individual drugs; spread it over two days.

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ questions | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

The question bank has long essay (10-mark), short answer (5-mark) and very short (2-mark) questions. Very short questions help with Section A and with quick revision.

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — asked in most years; prepare the full answer with tables, examples and a diagram where one fits.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from syllabus weight and common patterns in PCI-syllabus pharmacy papers, not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Introduction and evaluation | Definition and scope, classification of crude drugs (all seven systems), organised vs unorganised drugs, adulteration types, evaluation methods, leaf constants, lycopodium spore method |
| 2 Cultivation | Factors affecting cultivation, collection and drying, plant hormones, polyploidy, mutation, hybridisation, conservation |
| 3 Tissue culture | History, types of cultures, nutritional requirements (MS medium), growth measurement, applications, edible vaccines |
| 4 Systems of medicine and secondary metabolites | Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, Homeopathy, Chinese medicine; definition, classification and tests of alkaloids, glycosides, flavonoids, tannins, volatile oils, resins |
| 5 Drug monographs | Acacia, agar, tragacanth, honey, gelatin, castor oil, beeswax, wool fat, proteolytic enzymes, fibres, marine drugs, hallucinogens, teratogens, allergens |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. Every drug monograph has the same skeleton: **biological source with family → geographical source → collection/preparation → description → chemical constituents → tests → uses → adulterants or storage.** Write each heading even if you remember only one line under it.
2. Write the biological name in full the first time, genus with a capital letter and species in small letters (underline it in handwriting), followed by the family: *Acacia senegal*, Leguminosae.
3. For classification questions use a table with one example per class. Tables earn marks fast and are easy to check.
4. For identification tests give **reagent → observation → what it shows** (for example, Shinoda: Mg + HCl → pink/red → flavonoids).
5. Draw simple labelled diagrams: steps of tissue culture, the growth curve of a suspension culture, the lycopodium spore method, camera lucida set-up, auxin–cytokinin balance.
6. Learn the few formulas in this subject cold: stomatal index = S × 100/(E + S); lycopodium count = N × W × 94,000/(S × M); foaming index = 1000/a.
7. In 10-mark essays on evaluation, tissue culture or secondary metabolites, end with a short list of pharmaceutical applications — examiners look for the link to medicines.
8. Do not confuse similar pairs: organised vs unorganised drugs; hydrolysable vs condensed tannins; tragacanthin vs bassorin; agarose vs agaropectin; Type A vs Type B gelatin; urokinase vs streptokinase; stomatal number vs stomatal index.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you only have an hour, learn these five topics fully: **classification of crude drugs with examples**, **evaluation of crude drugs including leaf constants and the lycopodium method**, **plant tissue culture (types, medium, applications)**, **definition, classification and tests of alkaloids and glycosides**, and **monographs of acacia, tragacanth, agar, honey, castor oil and beeswax**. Together they cover most 10-mark questions.

**Unit 1 in one table**

| Topic | Key points |
| --- | --- |
| Pharmacognosy | *pharmakon* + *gnosis*; Seydler, 1815 |
| Organised drugs | Have cells: leaves, barks, roots, flowers, fruits, seeds |
| Unorganised drugs | No cells: latex (opium), juice (aloe), extract (catechu), gums, resins, balsams, waxes |
| Classifications | Alphabetical, morphological, taxonomical, chemical, pharmacological, chemotaxonomic, serotaxonomic |
| Evaluation | Organoleptic, microscopic, physical, chemical, biological |
| Stomata | Anomocytic (digitalis), anisocytic (belladonna), diacytic (vasaka), paracytic (senna) |
| Stomatal index | SI = S × 100/(E + S) |
| Lycopodium | ~94,000 spores/mg; particles/mg = N × W × 94,000/(S × M) |
| Ash values | Total, acid-insoluble (sand, silica), water-soluble, sulphated |

**Unit 2**

| Topic | Key points |
| --- | --- |
| Propagation | Seeds (sexual); cuttings, layering, grafting, budding, rhizomes, micropropagation (asexual) |
| Cultivation factors | Altitude, temperature, rainfall, light, soil, fertilisers, pests, genetics |
| Collection time | Leaves at flowering; barks in spring; roots in autumn; flowers as buds |
| Processing | Garbling, drying, curing (vanilla → vanillin), packing, storage |
| Hormones | Auxin (rooting), gibberellin (elongation), cytokinin (cell division, shoots), ABA (dormancy), ethylene (ripening) |
| Genetics | Colchicine → polyploidy; X-rays, gamma rays, EMS → mutation; crossing → hybrid vigour |
| Conservation | In situ (parks, reserves, sacred groves); ex situ (gardens, seed banks, cryopreservation at −196 °C) |

**Unit 3**

| Topic | Key points |
| --- | --- |
| History | Haberlandt 1902 (father); White 1934; Skoog & Miller 1957; MS medium 1962; Guha & Maheshwari 1964 |
| Types | Callus, suspension, organ, anther, protoplast, hairy root (*A. rhizogenes*), immobilised |
| Medium | Salts, sucrose 2–3%, vitamins, auxin + cytokinin, agar 0.6–1%, pH 5.6–5.8, autoclave 121 °C |
| Growth | Fresh/dry weight, packed cell volume, cell count; viability by fluorescein diacetate |
| Applications | Metabolites (shikonin), biotransformation (*Digitalis lanata*), micropropagation, virus-free plants, haploids, conservation |
| Edible vaccine | Antigen gene in edible plant (banana, potato, tomato); mucosal IgA immunity |

**Unit 4 tests to write without thinking**

| Group | Test | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Alkaloids | Mayer's / Dragendorff's / Wagner's / Hager's | Cream / orange / reddish-brown / yellow precipitate |
| Purine alkaloids | Murexide | Purple with ammonia |
| Cardiac glycosides | Keller–Killiani | Reddish-brown ring, bluish-green upper layer |
| Cardenolide ring | Legal / Baljet | Pink-red / orange |
| Anthraquinones | Borntrager's | Pink-red ammonia layer |
| Saponins | Froth test / haemolysis | Lasting froth / RBC lysis |
| Cyanogenetic glycosides | Sodium picrate paper | Brick red |
| Flavonoids | Shinoda (Mg + HCl) | Pink to magenta |
| Tannins | FeCl3; gelatin; goldbeater's skin | Blue-black or green-black; white precipitate; brown-black |
| Volatile oils | Filter-paper spot | No permanent grease mark |

Systems: Ayurveda (three doshas), Unani (four humours: dam, balgham, safra, sauda), Siddha (metals and minerals, Siddhars), Homeopathy (Hahnemann, like cures like), Chinese (yin–yang, qi; ephedrine, artemisinin).

**Unit 5 drug sources**

| Drug | Source (family) | Key constituent | Key use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Acacia | *Acacia senegal* (Leguminosae) | Arabin; oxidase | Emulsifier, suspending agent |
| Agar | *Gelidium*, *Gracilaria* (red algae) | Agarose, agaropectin | Culture media, laxative |
| Tragacanth | *Astragalus gummifer* (Leguminosae) | Tragacanthin, bassorin | Suspending agent |
| Honey | *Apis mellifera* (Apidae) | Invert sugar 70–80% | Demulcent, vehicle |
| Gelatin | Animal collagen | Glycine, proline, hydroxyproline | Capsules, haemostatic sponge |
| Casein | Milk | Phosphoprotein | Nutrient, emulsifier |
| Papain | *Carica papaya* latex (Caricaceae) | Cysteine protease | Digestant, debridement |
| Bromelain | *Ananas comosus* (Bromeliaceae) | Cysteine proteases | Anti-oedema |
| Streptokinase / urokinase | Group C streptococci / urine, kidney cells | Plasminogen activators | Thrombolysis |
| Castor oil | *Ricinus communis* (Euphorbiaceae) | Ricinoleic acid | Purgative, emollient |
| Chaulmoogra oil | *Hydnocarpus* spp. | Hydnocarpic, chaulmoogric acids | Leprosy (historical) |
| Wool fat | *Ovis aries* (Bovidae) | Sterol esters | Water-absorbing ointment base |
| Beeswax | *Apis mellifera* | Myricyl palmitate, cerotic acid | Stiffening agent, cold cream |
| Cotton / jute / hemp | *Gossypium* / *Corchorus* / *Cannabis sativa* | Cellulose / lignocellulose | Dressings / sacking / ropes |

Marine drugs: cytarabine (sponge), trabectedin (tunicate), eribulin (sponge), ziconotide (cone snail), cephalosporins (marine fungus), protamine (fish sperm).

**Last-minute traps**

- Bassorin swells but does not dissolve; tragacanthin dissolves.
- Castor oil is miscible with alcohol; chaulmoogra oil is dextrorotatory.
- Wool fat and beeswax are waxes, not fats (no glycerol).
- Streptokinase is not an enzyme itself; urokinase activates plasminogen directly.
- Acid-insoluble ash shows sand and earth; very low water-soluble ash suggests an exhausted drug.

# Analysis of crude drugs by chemical tests: tragacanth, acacia, agar, gelatin, starch, honey and castor oil

**Aim:** To identify tragacanth, acacia, agar, gelatin, starch, honey and castor oil by their characteristic chemical tests.

> Follow your lab manual and your teacher where details differ. Benzidine is a carcinogen: many laboratories now skip the benzidine test or use it only as a demonstration, wearing gloves.

## Principle

Unorganised drugs have no cells to examine under the microscope, so they are identified by physical behaviour (swelling, gel formation, solubility) and by chemical reactions of their main constituents:
- polysaccharides (gums, agar, starch) react with iodine, lead salts and dyes such as ruthenium red;
- proteins (gelatin) are precipitated by tannic acid and picric acid and give ammonia on heating with soda lime;
- reducing sugars (honey) reduce Fehling's solution, and fructose gives Seliwanoff's test;
- castor oil is identified by its unusual solubility in alcohol.

## Requirements

**Drugs:** samples of tragacanth, acacia, agar, gelatin, starch (maize or potato), honey and castor oil.

**Reagents:**
- iodine solution (0.1 N) and lead subacetate solution;
- ruthenium red solution and 20% sodium hydroxide solution;
- tannic acid solution (10%) and saturated picric acid solution;
- soda lime, Fehling's solutions A and B, and Seliwanoff's reagent (resorcinol in HCl);
- ethanol (95%) and light petroleum.

**Apparatus:** test tubes, water bath, beakers, glass rods, slides and microscope.

## Procedure and observations

| Drug | Test | Observation | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Tragacanth** | Add 1 g powder to 20 ml water and allow to stand | Swells to a stiff, translucent gel | Bassorin swells |
|  | Mount powder in iodine solution and examine | A few small blue starch grains | Traces of starch |
|  | Boil a little powder with 20% NaOH | Canary-yellow colour | Tragacanth |
|  | Mount powder in ruthenium red | Particles stain pink | Mucilage |
| **Acacia** | Dissolve 1 g in 2 ml water | Dissolves slowly to a viscous, clear solution | Water-soluble gum |
|  | Add lead subacetate to the solution | White precipitate | Arabin (polysaccharide) |
|  | Hydrolyse with dilute acid, neutralise, warm with Fehling's | Brick-red precipitate | Reducing sugars after hydrolysis |
|  | (Demonstration) solution + alcoholic benzidine + H2O2 | Blue colour | Oxidase enzyme |
| **Agar** | Boil 0.5 g in 30 ml water, cool | Clear solution sets to a firm gel | Agarose |
|  | Warm a little powder with iodine solution | Crimson to violet colour | Agar |
|  | Mount in ruthenium red | Pink | Mucilage |
|  | Add tannic acid to a warm 0.5% solution | No precipitate | Distinguishes agar from gelatin |
| **Gelatin** | Dissolve 1 g in 50 ml hot water; cool a portion | Sets to a gel | Gelatin |
|  | Add tannic acid to the warm solution | Buff/white precipitate | Protein |
|  | Add picric acid | Yellow precipitate | Protein |
|  | Heat solid gelatin with soda lime | Ammonia smell; moist red litmus turns blue | Nitrogen (protein) |
| **Starch** | Boil 1 g with 15 ml water and cool | Translucent viscous mucilage | Starch |
|  | Add iodine solution to the cooled mucilage | Deep blue; disappears on warming, returns on cooling | Starch–iodine complex |
|  | Mount powder in water and examine | Grains of typical shape and hilum | Identity of the starch source |
| **Honey** | Dilute 1 ml with 5 ml water, add Fehling's A + B, boil | Brick-red precipitate | Reducing sugars (invert sugar) |
|  | Warm with Seliwanoff's reagent | Red colour | Fructose |
|  | Fiehe's test on an ether extract with resorcinol–HCl | No cherry-red colour | Absence of artificial invert sugar |
| **Castor oil** | Shake 1 ml with 1 ml ethanol (95%) | Clear mixture | Miscible with alcohol (hydroxy fatty acid) |
|  | Shake 1 ml with 3 ml light petroleum | Turbid; does not mix completely | Only slightly soluble |
|  | Note viscosity | Very viscous | Ricinoleic acid glycerides |

## Result

The given samples were identified as tragacanth, acacia, agar, gelatin, starch, honey and castor oil by the tests above.

## Precautions

1. Use clean, dry test tubes and fresh reagents.
2. Add reagents drop by drop and note colours immediately.
3. Heat test tubes on a water bath, pointing away from yourself and others.
4. Handle benzidine and NaOH with gloves.

## Viva questions

1. **What makes tragacanth swell but not dissolve completely?** Bassorin, the water-insoluble fraction, swells to a gel; only tragacanthin dissolves.
2. **Why is acacia solution heated before use with some drugs?** To inactivate its oxidase enzyme, which can destroy easily oxidised drugs.
3. **How do you tell agar from gelatin?** Gelatin gives a precipitate with tannic acid; agar does not. Gelatin gives ammonia with soda lime; agar does not.
4. **Why does the blue starch–iodine colour vanish on warming?** Heat releases iodine from the helical amylose–iodine complex; it reforms on cooling.
5. **What does Fiehe's test detect?** Artificial invert sugar, through the hydroxymethylfurfural formed during its manufacture.
6. **Why is castor oil miscible with alcohol?** Its ricinoleic acid carries a hydroxyl group, making the oil more polar than other fixed oils.
7. **Name the two fractions of agar.** Agarose (gelling) and agaropectin (sulphated, non-gelling).

# Determination of stomatal number and stomatal index

**Aim:** To determine the stomatal number and stomatal index of the given leaf (for example senna or datura) on the upper and lower surfaces.

> Quantities and the leaf used follow your lab manual. Compare your values with those given in your manual for the drug, not with values from a different leaf.

## Principle

**Stomatal number** is the average number of stomata per square millimetre of epidermis. It changes with the age of the leaf, its position on the plant and growing conditions, so it is less reliable.

**Stomatal index (SI)** is the percentage of stomata out of the total number of epidermal cells and stomata in the same area:

**SI = S × 100 / (E + S)**

where S = number of stomata and E = number of ordinary epidermal cells in the same unit area. Since leaf area changes both E and S together, SI stays fairly constant for a species. It is used to identify a leaf drug and to separate closely related species (for example Indian and Alexandrian senna).

## Requirements

Fresh or dried leaves, chloral hydrate solution, glycerin, slides, cover slips, compound microscope, camera lucida, stage micrometer, drawing paper, sharp pencil, forceps, water bath.

## Procedure

1. Take small pieces of leaf from the middle part of the lamina, between midrib and margin.
2. Clear them by boiling with chloral hydrate solution on a water bath until transparent (or peel off the epidermis).
3. Mount the upper and lower epidermis separately in glycerin, with the surface uppermost.
4. Set up the camera lucida. Using the stage micrometer, draw a square of 1 mm × 1 mm to scale on the paper (or calibrate the field area).
5. Replace the stage micrometer with the specimen. Trace the epidermal cells and stomata falling inside the square.
6. Count the stomata (S) and the epidermal cells (E). Count a cell or stoma cut by the boundary only if more than half of it lies inside the square (or count those on two sides only).
7. Repeat for at least 10 fields on each surface and take the average.

## Observations and calculation

| Field | Surface | Epidermal cells (E) | Stomata (S) | SI = S × 100/(E + S) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Lower |  |  |  |
| 2 | Lower |  |  |  |
| … | … |  |  |  |
| 10 | Lower |  |  |  |
| Average |  |  |  |  |

Stomatal number = average S per mm².

**Worked example.** In one field (1 mm²) of the lower surface, E = 152 and S = 38.
SI = 38 × 100 / (152 + 38) = 3800/190 = **20.0**. The stomatal number for that field = 38 per mm².

## Result

Stomatal number of the given leaf: upper surface ___ /mm², lower surface ___ /mm².
Stomatal index: upper surface ___, lower surface ___.

## Precautions

1. Clear the leaf fully so cell outlines are sharp.
2. Use leaves from the middle of the lamina, avoiding the midrib and margins.
3. Keep the camera lucida setting unchanged once calibrated.
4. Count enough fields and take the average.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is stomatal index more reliable than stomatal number?** Leaf expansion changes the number per area, but stomata and epidermal cells increase together, so their ratio stays constant.
2. **Who introduced the stomatal index?** Salisbury (1927).
3. **Name the four common stomatal types with one example each.** Anomocytic (digitalis), anisocytic (belladonna), diacytic (vasaka), paracytic (senna).
4. **Why is chloral hydrate used?** It clears the tissue by dissolving starch, chlorophyll and other contents, making cell walls visible.
5. **Which surface usually has more stomata?** The lower surface in most dicot leaves.
6. **What is the use of these values?** Identification of leaf drugs, and detecting substitution with related species.

# Determination of vein-islet number, vein-termination number and palisade ratio

**Aim:** To determine the vein-islet number, vein-termination number and palisade ratio of the given leaf (for example senna, datura or digitalis).

> Follow your lab manual for the leaf and clearing method. Compare results with the values listed in your manual for that drug.

## Principle

- **Vein-islet** — the smallest area of photosynthetic tissue completely surrounded by veinlets.
- **Vein-islet number** — the average number of vein-islets per square millimetre of leaf surface, counted midway between the midrib and the margin.
- **Vein-termination number** — the average number of free veinlet endings per square millimetre.
- **Palisade ratio** — the average number of palisade cells beneath one upper epidermal cell.

These values are constant for a species and do not depend on the size of the leaf. They help identify whole and broken leaves and detect substitution with related species (for example *Cassia angustifolia* and *C. acutifolia*).

## Requirements

Leaves, chloral hydrate solution, glycerin, phloroglucinol and conc. HCl (optional, to stain veins red), slides, cover slips, compound microscope, camera lucida, stage micrometer, drawing paper.

## Procedure

**A. Vein-islet and vein-termination number**

1. Cut square pieces of leaf (about 2–3 mm) from the lamina midway between midrib and margin.
2. Clear by boiling in chloral hydrate solution until transparent; stain with phloroglucinol–HCl if needed so that veins show red.
3. Mount in glycerin.
4. With the camera lucida and stage micrometer, draw a square of **2 mm × 2 mm (4 mm²)** on the paper to scale.
5. Replace with the specimen and trace the veins inside the square.
6. Count the vein-islets in the square. Count islets cut by the top and left sides; ignore those cut by the bottom and right sides.
7. Count the vein terminations inside the square.
8. Divide by 4 to get the values per mm². Repeat for several pieces and average.

**B. Palisade ratio**

1. Clear small pieces of leaf in chloral hydrate and mount with the upper surface towards the objective.
2. Using the camera lucida, trace a group of **four** upper epidermal cells.
3. Focus down to the palisade layer and trace the palisade cells lying beneath these four cells. Count a palisade cell if more than half of it lies under the group.
4. Palisade ratio = number of palisade cells ÷ 4.
5. Repeat for at least 10 groups and take the average (also note the range).

## Observations and calculation

| Piece | Vein-islets in 4 mm² | Vein-islet number (/mm²) | Terminations in 4 mm² | Vein-termination number (/mm²) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 |  |  |  |  |
| 2 |  |  |  |  |
| 3 |  |  |  |  |
| Average |  |  |  |  |

| Group of 4 epidermal cells | Palisade cells beneath | Palisade ratio |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 |  |  |
| … |  |  |
| 10 |  |  |
| Average |  |  |

**Worked example.** In 4 mm², 96 vein-islets and 104 terminations were counted.
- Vein-islet number = 96/4 = **24 per mm²**.
- Vein-termination number = 104/4 = **26 per mm²**.

Under four epidermal cells, 30 palisade cells were counted, so palisade ratio = 30/4 = **7.5**.

## Result

For the given leaf:
- vein-islet number = ___ per mm²;
- vein-termination number = ___ per mm²;
- palisade ratio = ___ (range ___ to ___).

## Precautions

1. Take pieces only from midway between midrib and margin.
2. Clear completely so all veinlets are visible.
3. Do not change the camera lucida setting after calibration.
4. Follow a fixed rule for counting islets on the boundary.

## Viva questions

1. **Define vein-islet.** The smallest area of green tissue surrounded on all sides by veinlets.
2. **Who introduced vein-islet number?** Levin (1929).
3. **Why are these values useful?** They are constant for a species, independent of leaf size, and work even on broken leaf pieces.
4. **Why is the square drawn as 4 mm² rather than 1 mm²?** A larger area gives a more reliable average with fewer boundary errors.
5. **Where is the palisade ratio counted?** Under the upper epidermis, in groups of four epidermal cells.
6. **Why is phloroglucinol–HCl used?** It stains the lignified xylem of veins red, making them easy to trace.

# Determination of size of starch grains and calcium oxalate crystals by eyepiece micrometer

**Aim:** To calibrate an eyepiece micrometer and to measure the size of starch grains (for example potato, maize or rice starch) and calcium oxalate crystals (for example in senna or rhubarb powder).

> Follow your lab manual for the samples used. Record the objective used for each measurement, because the calibration factor differs for each objective.

## Principle

An **eyepiece micrometer** is a glass disc with an arbitrary scale (often 100 divisions) placed in the eyepiece. Its divisions have no fixed value; their real length depends on the objective in use. It is therefore calibrated against a **stage micrometer**, a slide on which 1 mm is divided into 100 parts, each equal to 0.01 mm = **10 µm**.

When lines of both scales coincide at two points:

**Value of one eyepiece division (µm) = (number of stage divisions × 10) / (number of eyepiece divisions)**

The size of an object = number of eyepiece divisions it covers × value of one eyepiece division.

## Requirements

Compound microscope, eyepiece micrometer, stage micrometer, slides, cover slips, starch powders, drug powder containing calcium oxalate (senna, rhubarb), water, glycerin, chloral hydrate solution.

## Procedure

**A. Calibration**

1. Unscrew the eye lens, place the eyepiece micrometer on the diaphragm (scale up) and replace the lens.
2. Place the stage micrometer on the stage and focus with the low-power objective, then with the high-power objective.
3. Rotate the eyepiece so both scales are parallel. Make the zero lines coincide.
4. Find another point further along where a line of the eyepiece scale exactly coincides with a line of the stage scale.
5. Count the divisions of each scale between the two coinciding points and calculate the value of one eyepiece division.

**B. Measurement**

1. Remove the stage micrometer.
2. Mount starch in water (or dilute glycerin). Mount calcium oxalate powder cleared in chloral hydrate.
3. Measure the length (and breadth) of at least 25 starch grains or crystals in eyepiece divisions. For starch, measure the longest axis.
4. Convert to micrometres and find the range and the average.

## Observations and calculation

**Calibration (high power):**

| Eyepiece divisions | Stage divisions | Value of one eyepiece division (µm) |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  |  |  |

**Measurements:**

| No. | Object | Eyepiece divisions | Size (µm) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Starch grain |  |  |
| … | … |  |  |
| 25 |  |  |  |

**Worked example.** 40 eyepiece divisions coincide with 10 stage divisions.
Value of one eyepiece division = (10 × 10) / 40 = **2.5 µm**.
A starch grain covering 18 eyepiece divisions measures 18 × 2.5 = **45 µm**.

## Result

- Value of one eyepiece division at ___× objective = ___ µm.
- Size of starch grains of ___ = ___ to ___ µm (average ___ µm).
- Size of calcium oxalate crystals in ___ = ___ to ___ µm (average ___ µm).

## Precautions

1. Calibrate separately for each objective and do not change the objective or the eyepiece after calibration.
2. Choose coinciding lines as far apart as possible for accuracy.
3. Measure grains lying flat, and enough of them to give a fair range.
4. Clean the stage micrometer gently; its scale is easily scratched.

## Viva questions

1. **Why must the eyepiece micrometer be calibrated?** Its divisions have no fixed value; their real size depends on the objective magnification.
2. **What is the value of one stage micrometer division?** 0.01 mm, that is 10 µm.
3. **How do you identify potato starch?** Large, oval to egg-shaped simple grains with an eccentric hilum and clear concentric striations.
4. **How do you identify maize starch?** Polygonal simple grains with a central star-shaped (stellate) hilum.
5. **How do you confirm calcium oxalate?** It is insoluble in acetic acid and dissolves in HCl without effervescence.
6. **Name the shapes of calcium oxalate crystals.** Prisms, rosettes (clusters), acicular raphides and microsphenoidal (sandy) crystals.
practicals.title: Size of starch grains and calcium oxalate crystals by eyepiece micrometer

# Determination of fibre length and width

**Aim:** To determine the length and width of fibres in the given drug or fibre sample (for example cotton, jute, or fibres from a bark such as cinchona or cinnamon).

> Follow your lab manual for the maceration method. Schultze's reagent is a strong oxidant: use it in a fume hood, away from organic matter, with gloves and goggles.

## Principle

Fibres are long, narrow, thick-walled cells. Their length and width are fairly constant for a given drug and help identify it and detect adulteration. In a tissue the fibres are held together, so they are first separated by **maceration**:
- with Schultze's reagent (potassium chlorate in nitric acid), which dissolves the middle lamella, or
- for soft tissues, by boiling with dilute alkali.

The separated fibres are measured with a calibrated eyepiece micrometer:
- length usually under low power (or by projecting with a camera lucida);
- width under high power.

## Requirements

Fibre or drug sample, potassium chlorate, conc. nitric acid (or 50% nitric acid), water, glycerin, test tubes, water bath, needles, slides, cover slips, microscope, eyepiece and stage micrometers, camera lucida.

## Procedure

1. Calibrate the eyepiece micrometer for the low-power and high-power objectives (see the eyepiece micrometer practical).
2. Cut the material into small pieces. For cotton, simply tease out a few fibres; maceration is not needed.
3. Macerate: warm the pieces with a few crystals of potassium chlorate and 50% nitric acid until the tissue softens and separates (Schultze's maceration).
4. Pour off the acid, wash the pieces several times with water, and tease them apart with needles.
5. Mount the separated fibres in dilute glycerin.
6. Measure the length of at least 25 complete (unbroken) fibres under low power. For long fibres, trace them with the camera lucida and measure the tracing against a traced stage micrometer scale.
7. Measure the width of the same fibres at the middle under high power.
8. Note the shape of the fibre ends, lumen and wall thickness, and lignification (stain with phloroglucinol–HCl).

## Observations and calculation

Value of one eyepiece division: low power ___ µm; high power ___ µm.

| Fibre | Length (eyepiece divisions) | Length (µm) | Width (eyepiece divisions) | Width (µm) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 |  |  |  |  |
| … |  |  |  |  |
| 25 |  |  |  |  |
| Range / average |  |  |  |  |

**Worked example.** Low power: one eyepiece division = 15 µm. A fibre covers 42 divisions, so its length = 42 × 15 = **630 µm**. High power: one division = 2.5 µm; width = 10 divisions = **25 µm**.

## Result

- Length of fibres = ___ to ___ µm (average ___ µm).
- Width = ___ to ___ µm (average ___ µm).
- The fibres are ___ (lignified / not lignified).

## Precautions

1. Measure only complete fibres; broken ones give low values.
2. Do not over-macerate, or the fibres will break.
3. Wash off all the acid before mounting.
4. Calibrate for each objective used.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the purpose of maceration?** To dissolve the middle lamella so that individual fibres separate.
2. **Composition of Schultze's maceration fluid?** Potassium chlorate with nitric acid.
3. **How does cotton differ from jute under the microscope?** Cotton is a single flattened, twisted, unlignified cell; jute fibres are lignified bast cells with an irregular lumen.
4. **How do you test for lignin?** Phloroglucinol with conc. HCl stains lignified walls pink to red.
5. **Which fibre is used for absorbent cotton?** The seed hairs of *Gossypium* species.
6. **Why measure many fibres?** Fibre size varies, so a range and an average from many fibres are reliable.
practicals.title: Fibre length and width

# Determination of number of starch grains by the lycopodium spore method

**Aim:** To determine the number of starch grains per mg of the given powdered drug (for example powdered ginger) and its purity by the lycopodium spore method.

> Follow your lab manual for the amounts and the suspending liquid. Work out the purity only if a standard (genuine) sample has been counted the same way.

## Principle

Lycopodium spores (from *Lycopodium clavatum*) are very uniform in size and shape, and **1 mg contains about 94,000 spores**. A known weight of lycopodium is mixed with a known weight of the powdered drug, and the spores serve as an internal standard. By counting, in the same fields, the spores and a characteristic countable element of the drug (starch grains, oil cells, pollen grains), the number of such elements in 1 mg of the drug is found:

**Number of starch grains per mg = (N × W × 94,000) / (S × M)**

where:
- N = starch grains counted,
- S = lycopodium spores counted in the same fields,
- W = weight of lycopodium (mg),
- M = weight of drug (mg).

**% purity = (starch grains per mg of sample / starch grains per mg of genuine drug) × 100**

## Requirements

Powdered drug, lycopodium spores (dried), mucilage of tragacanth or a suitable suspending liquid, glycerin, water, mortar and pestle, analytical balance, slides, cover slips (large), microscope.

## Procedure

1. Accurately weigh about 100 mg of the powdered drug (M) and about 50 mg of lycopodium (W).
2. Mix them thoroughly in a mortar with a little mucilage, then dilute with water or glycerin–water to a known volume, so the suspension is uniform.
3. Place one drop of the well-shaken suspension on a slide, cover with a large cover slip, and examine under the microscope.
4. In each of at least 25 fields, count the lycopodium spores (S) and the starch grains (N) of the drug.
5. Total the counts over all fields and calculate.

## Observations and calculation

| Field | Lycopodium spores (S) | Starch grains (N) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 |  |  |
| … |  |  |
| 25 |  |  |
| Total |  |  |

**Worked example.** M = 100 mg drug, W = 50 mg lycopodium. Over 25 fields, S = 400 spores and N = 1,000 starch grains.

Starch grains per mg = (1,000 × 50 × 94,000) / (400 × 100) = 4,700,000,000 / 40,000 = **117,500 per mg**.

If the genuine drug gives 125,000 per mg, purity = 117,500/125,000 × 100 = **94%**.

## Result

- Number of starch grains in the given powdered drug = ___ per mg.
- Purity of the sample = ___%.

## Precautions

1. Weigh both the drug and lycopodium accurately.
2. Mix thoroughly so that the suspension is uniform; shake before taking each drop.
3. Count enough fields (at least 25) to reduce error.
4. Use a fixed rule for objects on the edge of the field.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is lycopodium used as the standard?** Its spores are very uniform in size and shape and of known number per mg.
2. **How many spores are there in 1 mg of lycopodium?** About 94,000.
3. **What shape are lycopodium spores?** Tetrahedral with a reticulate (net-like) surface, about 25 µm across.
4. **For what kind of drugs is this method used?** Powdered drugs where a characteristic element can be counted, such as starch grains in ginger, oil cells or pollen grains.
5. **What else can the method measure?** The proportion of an adulterant, if the adulterant has a countable feature (e.g., foreign starch).
6. **Why not simply weigh the starch?** Starch cannot be separated quantitatively from the powder; counting against a standard is easier and accurate.
practicals.title: Number of starch grains by the lycopodium spore method

# Determination of ash values of a crude drug

**Aim:** To determine the total ash, acid-insoluble ash and water-soluble ash of the given powdered crude drug.

> Follow the method and limits in your lab manual or the pharmacopoeia monograph for the drug used. Handle hot crucibles with tongs and let them cool in a desiccator before weighing.

## Principle

When a crude drug is incinerated, the organic matter burns away and an inorganic residue (**ash**) is left.

| Value | What it measures | Significance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Total ash** | All inorganic matter: natural salts of the plant (physiological ash) plus adhering earth and sand (non-physiological ash) | High value suggests contamination or adulteration with earthy matter |
| **Acid-insoluble ash** | Residue after boiling the total ash with dilute HCl: mainly silica | Measures sand and soil contamination; more useful than total ash for drugs naturally rich in calcium oxalate |
| **Water-soluble ash** | Part of total ash dissolved by water | Very low value suggests an exhausted drug (soluble salts removed by previous extraction) |

## Requirements

Powdered drug (passed through a sieve), silica or platinum crucible with lid, muffle furnace or burner, analytical balance, desiccator, ashless filter paper, dilute hydrochloric acid (about 2 M), distilled water, tongs, water bath, funnel.

## Procedure

**A. Total ash**

1. Heat an empty crucible to redness, cool in a desiccator, and weigh. Repeat until the weight is constant.
2. Accurately weigh about 2–3 g of the powdered drug into the crucible.
3. Spread it evenly. Heat gently at first, then raise the temperature gradually, not above about 450 °C, until the ash is free from carbon (white or grey).
4. If carbon persists, cool, moisten the residue with hot water, dry on a water bath, and ignite again.
5. Cool in a desiccator and weigh. Repeat heating, cooling and weighing to constant weight.

**B. Acid-insoluble ash**

1. Boil the total ash with 25 ml of dilute HCl for 5 minutes.
2. Collect the insoluble matter on an ashless filter paper and wash it with hot water until free from acid.
3. Transfer the paper with residue to the tared crucible. Dry, ignite to constant weight, cool and weigh.

**C. Water-soluble ash**

1. Boil the total ash with 25 ml of water for 5 minutes.
2. Collect the insoluble matter on an ashless filter paper and wash with hot water.
3. Ignite the paper and residue in the tared crucible for 15 minutes at a temperature not above 450 °C, cool and weigh.
4. Subtract this weight from the weight of total ash. The difference is the water-soluble ash.

## Observations and calculation

| Item | Weight (g) |
| --- | --- |
| Empty crucible (W1) |  |
| Crucible + drug (W2) |  |
| Crucible + total ash (W3) |  |
| Crucible + acid-insoluble ash (W4) |  |
| Crucible + water-insoluble ash (W5) |  |

Weight of drug = W2 − W1

- % total ash = (W3 − W1) × 100 / (W2 − W1)
- % acid-insoluble ash = (W4 − W1) × 100 / (W2 − W1)
- % water-soluble ash = [(W3 − W1) − (W5 − W1)] × 100 / (W2 − W1)

**Worked example.** Drug taken = 2.000 g. Total ash = 0.140 g, acid-insoluble ash = 0.020 g, water-insoluble ash = 0.090 g.

- Total ash = 0.140 × 100/2 = **7.0% w/w**
- Acid-insoluble ash = 0.020 × 100/2 = **1.0% w/w**
- Water-soluble ash = (0.140 − 0.090) × 100/2 = **2.5% w/w**

## Result

The given drug has:
- total ash ___% w/w,
- acid-insoluble ash ___% w/w,
- water-soluble ash ___% w/w.

Compare these with the official limits for the drug.

## Precautions

1. Heat gently at first so the powder does not puff out of the crucible.
2. Do not exceed about 450 °C, since some salts (chlorides, carbonates) volatilise or decompose at higher temperatures.
3. Always cool in a desiccator before weighing, because hot ash takes up moisture.
4. Use ashless filter paper only.
5. Heat to constant weight.

## Viva questions

1. **What is physiological ash?** Ash from the plant's own inorganic constituents.
2. **What is non-physiological ash?** Ash from adhering soil and sand.
3. **Why is acid-insoluble ash important?** It measures silica (sand and earth) contamination, since natural plant salts dissolve in dilute HCl.
4. **What does a very low water-soluble ash suggest?** That the drug has been exhausted (extracted) before sale.
5. **What is sulphated ash?** Ash obtained after treating the drug with sulphuric acid before ignition; it converts salts to sulphates for a more constant value.
6. **Why does a drug like rhubarb have high total ash?** It contains much calcium oxalate, which leaves calcium oxide or carbonate.
7. **Why use ashless filter paper?** It leaves no measurable residue on burning.
practicals.title: Ash values (total, acid-insoluble, water-soluble)

# Determination of extractive values of crude drugs

**Aim:** To determine the alcohol-soluble and water-soluble extractive values of the given powdered crude drug.

> Follow your lab manual or the pharmacopoeia monograph for the solvent and strength of alcohol specified for the drug. Ethanol is flammable: evaporate on a water bath, never over a naked flame.

## Principle

The **extractive value** is the amount of material extracted from a known weight of drug by a particular solvent under fixed conditions, expressed as % w/w of the air-dried drug. It gives an idea of the amount of active or characteristic constituents, especially when no chemical assay exists.
- An exhausted or adulterated drug gives a lower value.
- Water extracts sugars, gums, tannins, glycosides and salts.
- Alcohol extracts resins, alkaloids, glycosides, tannins and some fats.
- Ether (volatile and non-volatile) extracts fats, volatile oils and resins.

## Requirements

Powdered drug (coarse powder), ethanol (90% or as specified), chloroform water (water saturated with chloroform, to prevent microbial growth during maceration), 250 ml stoppered conical flasks, measuring cylinders, filter paper, funnel, pipette (25 ml), tared flat-bottomed evaporating dish, water bath, hot-air oven at 105 °C, desiccator, analytical balance.

## Procedure

**A. Alcohol-soluble extractive**

1. Accurately weigh about 5 g of coarsely powdered drug into a stoppered flask.
2. Add 100 ml of ethanol of the specified strength.
3. Macerate for 24 hours: shake frequently during the first 6 hours, then allow to stand for 18 hours.
4. Filter rapidly, taking care to avoid loss of solvent.
5. Pipette 25 ml of the filtrate into a tared flat-bottomed dish and evaporate to dryness on a water bath.
6. Dry the residue at 105 °C to constant weight, cool in a desiccator, and weigh.

**B. Water-soluble extractive**

Proceed in the same way, using 100 ml of chloroform water instead of ethanol.

## Observations and calculation

| Item | Alcohol | Water |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Weight of drug (g) |  |  |
| Empty dish (g) |  |  |
| Dish + residue from 25 ml (g) |  |  |
| Weight of residue (g) |  |  |

Since 25 ml is one-quarter of the 100 ml used:

**% extractive = (weight of residue × 4 × 100) / weight of drug**

**Worked example.** 5.000 g drug macerated with 100 ml ethanol; 25 ml of filtrate gave 0.150 g residue.

% alcohol-soluble extractive = 0.150 × 4 × 100 / 5 = **12.0% w/w**

## Result

The given drug has:
- alcohol-soluble extractive ___% w/w,
- water-soluble extractive ___% w/w.

Compare these with the official limits.

## Precautions

1. Use the correct particle size and the exact solvent strength stated for the drug.
2. Keep the flask stoppered during maceration to prevent solvent loss.
3. Filter rapidly and cover the funnel to reduce evaporation.
4. Dry the residue to constant weight and cool in a desiccator before weighing.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the significance of extractive value?** It estimates the soluble constituents of a drug and helps detect exhausted or adulterated samples.
2. **Why is chloroform water used for the water-soluble extractive?** Chloroform acts as a preservative and prevents microbial growth during the 24-hour maceration.
3. **Why shake for 6 hours and then let stand for 18 hours?** To bring the solvent and drug to equilibrium in a standard, reproducible way.
4. **What is the difference between volatile and non-volatile ether-soluble extractive?** Volatile extractive is mainly volatile oil, lost on drying; non-volatile extractive includes fixed oils and resins.
5. **Why is only 25 ml of filtrate evaporated?** It is an aliquot; the value is multiplied by 4 for the full 100 ml.
6. **Why dry at 105 °C?** To remove the solvent and moisture completely without decomposing most constituents.
practicals.title: Extractive values (alcohol- and water-soluble)

# Determination of moisture content of crude drugs (loss on drying)

**Aim:** To determine the moisture content of the given powdered crude drug by the loss on drying method.

> Follow your lab manual for the weight of sample and drying temperature. For drugs rich in volatile oil, the toluene distillation method is used instead, because oven drying would also drive off the oil.

## Principle

Crude drugs always contain some water. Too much water:
- allows moulds and bacteria to grow,
- lets enzymes break down constituents (for example glycosides),
- adds useless weight.

The **loss on drying** is the loss in weight, expressed as % w/w, when the drug is dried at a fixed temperature (usually 105 °C) to constant weight. It measures water plus any other matter that is volatile at that temperature.

For drugs containing volatile oils (clove, fennel), moisture is found by **azeotropic (toluene) distillation**:
- the drug is distilled with water-immiscible toluene;
- water distils with the toluene and collects in a graduated receiver (Dean–Stark type) under the toluene layer, where its volume is read.

## Requirements

Powdered drug, tared flat glass-stoppered weighing bottle (or Petri dish), hot-air oven at 105 °C, desiccator with fresh desiccant, analytical balance, tongs.

## Procedure

1. Dry an empty weighing bottle with its stopper at 105 °C for 30 minutes, cool in a desiccator, and weigh (W1).
2. Place about 2–5 g of the powdered drug in the bottle, spread evenly, and weigh accurately (W2).
3. Dry in the oven at 105 °C with the stopper removed and kept beside the bottle.
4. After the set time (for example 2 hours), close the stopper, cool in a desiccator, and weigh.
5. Repeat drying for 30-minute periods until two successive weighings agree within 0.5 mg (constant weight) (W3).

## Observations and calculation

| Item | Weight (g) |
| --- | --- |
| Empty bottle (W1) |  |
| Bottle + drug before drying (W2) |  |
| Bottle + drug after drying to constant weight (W3) |  |

**% loss on drying = (W2 − W3) × 100 / (W2 − W1)**

**Worked example.** W1 = 25.300 g, W2 = 28.300 g (3.000 g drug), W3 = 28.060 g.
Loss = 0.240 g; % loss on drying = 0.240 × 100/3.000 = **8.0% w/w**.

## Result

The moisture content (loss on drying) of the given drug is ___% w/w.

## Precautions

1. Keep the layer of powder thin so drying is even.
2. Always cool in a desiccator with the stopper closed before weighing, since dried drug picks up moisture quickly.
3. Dry to constant weight.
4. Do not use this method for drugs rich in volatile oil.
5. Handle hot bottles with tongs; do not touch them with fingers, which adds moisture and grease.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is moisture content important?** Excess moisture favours microbial growth and enzyme action, lowers potency and adds weight.
2. **Why 105 °C?** It is just above the boiling point of water, removing water without decomposing most constituents.
3. **What does loss on drying measure besides water?** Any other matter volatile at the drying temperature.
4. **Which method is used for drugs containing volatile oil?** Toluene (azeotropic) distillation in a Dean–Stark apparatus.
5. **Name a chemical method for water content.** Karl Fischer titration, based on the reaction of iodine and sulphur dioxide with water.
6. **What is meant by constant weight?** Two successive weighings after further drying differ by not more than 0.5 mg.
practicals.title: Moisture content (loss on drying)
